claims.text: A two-phase coexistence molecular-dynamics method using DFT-calibrated interatomic potentials can estimate the melting properties of high-melting refractory materials accurately.
The method can estimate melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
The proposed method dramatically reduces computational cost relative to full ab initio free-energy integration.
The starting refractory material is equilibrated as a solid near its expected melting temperature.
The simulation contains coexisting solid and liquid regions and uses an interatomic potential benchmarked against DFT data.
The simulation is conducted under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions near the melting point.
Solid and liquid phases coexist in a single simulation cell.
A solid-liquid interface forms naturally in the coexistence simulation.
The solid-liquid interface mediates phase equilibrium and extraction of latent heat.
Simultaneous solid-liquid coexistence directly captures equilibrium at the melting point.
Latent heat, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change can be determined from the coexistence conditions.
The coexistence method avoids the step-by-step thermodynamic integration required by ab initio free-energy methods.
Predicted melting temperatures and thermodynamic discontinuities will agree closely with experimental values and full ab initio predictions.
The coexistence method will require only a fraction of the computational resources used by full ab initio calculations.
Full ab initio free-energy integration using DFT molecular dynamics is highly accurate.
Full ab initio free-energy integration is too computationally expensive for high-throughput use.
The proposed approach is effective only if the DFT-calibrated potential accurately represents both solid and liquid phases.
Failure to represent the complex bonding or energy landscape of refractory systems can cause errors in predicted latent heat and volume change.
A deviation greater than 5% from full ab initio and experimental reference values is proposed as a falsification threshold.
Failure to provide a significant computational speed-up would falsify the claim that the method is a high-throughput viable alternative.
